howtospecialist-16x20-gable.confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH on the lumber, sheet-goods, siding and roofing subtotal, which is ~85% of the dollars. Reasons: (1) every unit price on those lines came from a retailer page I fetched myself, and I re-verified the two largest lines (T1-11 $50.99 and 3/4 plywood $42.99) on a second fetch reading the schema.org ld+json offer directly; (2) two geographically independent live retailers, fetched the same day, agree within 3% on 3/4 in. plywood and within 16% on 2x4, with an archived Menards big-box stud price sitting between them — three-way corroboration on the commodity core; (3) all quantities on those lines are the plan's OWN published shopping list, not my take-off; (4) FRED WPU0811 confirms the price level is current rather than stale. MEDIUM on the total. Reasons it is not higher: the plan publishes zero counts for joist hangers, rafter ties, screws, nails, hinges and glue, so ~$500-700 of hardware rests on my take-offs and estimates rather than the plan; roofing nails could not be priced at all; the drip-edge unit price is a year-old archived Menards figure; the Dunn 4x4 skid price is extrapolated per-foot from an 8 ft post because they do not stock 20 ft; and the plan's own internal contradiction (192 in. cut list vs 20 ft shopping list on skids and rim joists) means the footprint the bill actually builds is not fully settled. LOW confidence specifically on the nails/staples line and the glue/filler placeholder — those two are marked as estimates and together are worth about $150, so they cannot move the headline much. Home Depot and Lowe's being unreachable is the main gap I could not close; I would not present this as a big-box cart price.
excludes: Foundation prep entirely: gravel bed, compaction, ground cloth, site levelling, excavation. The plan says 'leveled, compacted gravel bed' and buys nothing for it. Budget roughly $250-700 delivered for 6-8 cu yd of crushed rock on a 16x20 pad.
Concrete, piers, footings, anchors, hold-downs and tie-downs of any kind. The plan is 4x4 skids on gravel with no anchoring detail published.
Permits, plan-check fees, inspections. At 320 sq ft this is over the usual 100-200 sq ft exempt threshold, so a permit is very likely — commonly $150-800 depending on jurisdiction.

Engineering. The eleven 16 ft clear-span site-built 2x6/plywood-gusset trusses are not stamped. If a plan checker demands calculations, expect $400-1,500 for an engineer, or the cost of buying manufactured trusses instead.

Delivery. A 320 sq ft shed bill is roughly 3,000-3,500 lb of lumber plus 24 sheets of siding, 26 sheets of 3/4 plywood and 16 bundles of shingles — well past pickup-truck territory. Typical yard delivery $75-250.
Sales tax (0% to ~10% depending on state — on a $6,000 bill that is up to ~$600).
All tools: miter saw, circular saw, jigsaw, drill/driver, pocket-hole jig, chalk line, levels, ladders and scaffold, plus roof-safety gear.
Labor. Everything here is materials only. The plan's claimed 'one day' per part is fantasy for 320 sq ft with 11 site-built trusses.
Paint or stain, primer, caulk and brushes. The plan mentions 'stain/paint' but buys none. T1-11 must be finished: ~24 sheets = ~770 sq ft of wall, roughly 8-12 gallons for two coats, about $300-600.

Housewrap / weather-resistive barrier and structural shear sheathing. The plan puts 5/8 T1-11 straight on studs at 24 in. OC with no housewrap and no plywood shear panels — if your code requires either, add ~$700-1,200.
Insulation, vapor barrier, interior wall/ceiling finish, interior paint, shelving, workbenches.
Electrical of any kind: trenching, conduit, feeder, subpanel, receptacles, lighting, permits and electrician labor. For a detached 320 sq ft shop this is commonly $1,500-4,000 on its own.
Ridge vent, soffit vents, gable vents or any roof ventilation — none is specified in the plan.
Starter strip and hip/ridge cap shingles (the 16 bundles cover field area; a starter course is normally a separate product), and roof sealant/flashing cement.
Ramp, threshold, door sweep, door handles/pulls beyond the single latch, and any lock/hasp upgrade.
Gutters and downspouts.
Waste, breakage and miscut allowance. Every quantity here is the plan's published count with no overage factor; real jobs run 5-10% over.

mwps-75265-16x20-milkhouse.caveats:
SHORT ANSWER: buying this FREE plan and building it to spec at a Midwest lumber yard in September 2026 costs roughly $4,300-$6,600 in materials above grade, or $13.47-$20.72 per sq ft on 320 sq ft. Add ~$1,900-$2,600 for concrete + rebar and you are at roughly $6,200-$9,200 all-in on materials — still well under half the $11,000-$15,000 kit price, and the kit does not include a slab either.

WHAT LOW vs HIGH MEANS HERE. Both ends are REAL 2026 prices from the same retailer, Sutherlands, a Midwest yard with ~49 stores. LOW = the cheapest store's price on the value-grade option (SPF/SYP #2, 7/16 OSB, 11/32 T1-11, 3-tab shingles, blown cellulose). HIGH = an expensive store's price on the upgraded option (#2 Douglas Fir, 15/32 CDX plywood, 19/32 T1-11, architectural shingles, primed-panel lining, R-30 batts). I could NOT get a single 2026 big-box unit price — Home Depot, Lowe's, Menards and McCoy's all block requests and the Wayback Machine has no Home Depot product capture after 2023-09-25 and no Lowe's product captures at all. So the high column is NOT a big-box number. Directional evidence that big-box is dearer: Home Depot's 2x4x8 Prime Whitewood Stud was $7.98 in a 2023-09-25 archive versus $3.98-$4.29 at Sutherlands today, and FRED WPU0811 softwood-lumber PPI is up ~15% since then. Treat $6,600 as a yard ceiling; a Home-Depot-only build of the same bill would plausibly land higher. Also note the store-to-store spread inside Sutherlands runs past my high on several lines (19/32 T1-11 up to $59.99/sheet, the R-13 23\" bag up to $149.89) — an unlucky store adds several hundred dollars.

IS THE SPEC HEAVIER? Not structurally — it is LIGHTER than a modern shed plan. 2x4 studs at 24\" o.c. (not 16\"), 3/8\" roof sheathing (not 7/16\"/1/2\"), site-cut 2x6 rafters, no hurricane ties, no snow/wind table, no truss design. What makes it expensive is the INTERIOR: this is a dairy milkhouse, so it carries R-14 walls, R-23 ceiling, a 4-mil vapor barrier, a washable wall lining and a finished ceiling. Those five items plus the screen door, floor drains and removable panels are $1,466-$2,506 of the total — over a third. Strip them and build the same shell freestanding, unlined and uninsulated and you get $2,843-$4,124, i.e. $8.89-$12.89 per sq ft. That is the number most shed builders actually want.

THE PLAN IS ONLY THREE WALLS. This is the single biggest gotcha and it is easy to miss. The 16 ft gable endwall at the top of FLOOR PLAN 1/1 is labeled \"BARN\" and the estimating list states in plain text \"List does not include one endwall (existing barn wall) or material to extend roof to existing barn roof.\" My headline total therefore = the plan's own list ($3,779-$5,830) PLUS a fourth-endwall adder I built myself ($530-$800). If you actually have a barn to butt against, use the lower figure.

THE RAFTER COUNT IN THE PLAN IS WRONG (or at best ambiguous). The estimating list reads \"Rafters: 2x6's, 10 ft long ....... 11\" and \"Joists: 2x6's, 16 ft long ....... 11\". Eleven joists is exactly right for 24\" o.c. across a 20 ft building. But eleven rafter positions need TWO rafters each, one per slope — 22 pieces. I priced 22. If you order off the printed list you will be 11 rafters short (about $80-$145). The ridge board (2x6 x 20 ft), the felt underlayment and the drip edge are also missing from the estimating list entirely; I added all three.

CEILING JOIST SPAN IS AT THE LIMIT. A 2x6 at 24\" o.c. spanning the full 16 ft is right at the edge of modern IRC ceiling-joist tables for an uninhabitable attic with no storage. It is not obviously illegal, but it has essentially no margin, and if you ever put anything on that ceiling it fails. The plan's own title page says it \"provides conceptual information only\" and that professional services will be required including \"assurance of compliance with codes and regulations.\" Get it checked before you buy 2x6es.

SPEC SUBSTITUTIONS I MADE, ALL FLAGGED. (1) 3/8\" C-C Ext plywood with medium-density overlay (MDO) is effectively a special-order product now — no fetchable retailer stocks it — so siding is priced as APA T1-11 and the lining/ceiling as 15/32 CDX (low) or a 3/8\" B-grade primed panel (high). (2) 3/8\" C-C Ext 20/0 roof sheathing no longer exists in the trade; 7/16 OSB and 15/32 CDX both exceed it. (3) The plan's windows are site-built from 22\" x 24\" double-strength glass, which nobody prices online — I substituted small vinyl units at $114-$120 each, which OVERSTATES this line; building them per the plan is much cheaper. (4) The plan's deep-seal dairy floor drains are priced as $11 PVC drains, which UNDERSTATES them.

TWO LINES ARE NOT REAL PRICES, hence priced=PARTIAL: the 3/8\" x 10\" anchor bolts ($35-$50) and the quarter-round/glazing trim lot ($20-$30). Both are explicitly marked ESTIMATE in their source field. Together they are under 2% of the total. The removable-panel lot and the fourth-wall rake roof extension are derived/estimated from real unit prices. Everything else is a retailer-quoted 2026 figure.

TIMING RISK. FRED WPU0811 shows softwood lumber at 300.6 in July 2026, up from 250.1 in December 2025 — a ~20% run-up in seven months, and the highest reading in the series since the 2021-22 spike. These prices are a snapshot on a rising market; re-quote before you order.

myoutdoorplans-16x20-gable.confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH on the unit prices, MEDIUM on the total. High confidence on prices: 26 of 28 lines come from two live, directly-fetchable retailer catalogs (Sutherlands, snapshot-dated on-page 'as of Mon, Sep 7, 2026'; Dunn Lumber, fetched 2026-09-08), every SKU number and URL is recorded, and I re-scraped all of them a second time with a stricter parser after catching the first one pulling prices out of a 'Compare with Similar Items' carousel - so no price here is a mis-scrape of a neighbouring product. The two independent yards agree closely where they overlap (3/4in plywood $41.88 Dunn vs $42.99 Sutherlands), and FRED WPU081 corroborates the elevated level. Lower confidence on the total, for three reasons: (1) the plan publishes a cut list, not a shopping list, so the board/sheet counts are my cut plan and could vary a few percent; (2) three material groups (floor joists, truss gussets, all connectors and hinges) are absent from the published list and I supplied the quantities, which is about $500-$650 of the total; (3) there is no big-box price anywhere in it, so the low-high spread reflects grade and regional-yard choice rather than retailer channel. Treat $4,800-$6,900 as the materials bill and expect $5,500-$8,000 all-in once tax, delivery and a gravel pad are added - and note it is NOT a project budget: no foundation, permits, paint, tools or labor are in the number.
excludes: Sales tax - zero tax in the number. At 7-9% that is another $340-$620.
Delivery. A 1,900 board-foot, ~50-sheet order will not fit in a pickup. Yard delivery is typically $75-$250 per drop in this market, and none of it is in the total.

Foundation of any kind below the skids: gravel pad, crushed rock, landscape fabric, concrete blocks/piers/footings, ground anchors or tie-downs. The plan only says 'gravel, concrete or blocks' with no depth, spacing or quantity, so there is nothing to price. A 320 sq ft compacted gravel pad is commonly $400-$1,200 delivered.

Permits, plan review, engineering. At 320 sq ft this building exceeds the usual 100-200 sq ft exemption, and the 16ft site-built plywood-gusset trusses carry no stamp and no snow/wind rating, so a permitted jurisdiction may force engineered trusses - which would replace the 11 truss chord + 30 rafter + 44 web lines above with a truss package.
Labor. The plan's own page suggests $3,000-$5,000 for professional labor.
All tools: miter saw, circular saw, pocket-hole jig, drill/impact, ladders, truss jig, nailer or compressor, safety gear.
Housewrap, building paper, or any separate wall sheathing layer. The plan puts 5/8in T1-11 straight on the studs with nothing behind it.
Paint, primer, stain or sealer. T1-11 must be finished or it will fail; 640 sq ft of wall plus 8 trim boards is roughly 5-8 gallons.
Insulation, vapor barrier, interior wall/ceiling finish, interior floor covering.
Electrical: service feed, trenching, conduit, panel/subpanel, receptacles, lighting, switches.
Roof and soffit ventilation, ridge vent, gable vents, and any soffit/vented soffit material - none is specified anywhere in the free build.
Gutters and downspouts.
Front ramp and planter boxes (those are behind the $11.99 Gumroad PDF and are not in the free cut list).
Ice-and-water shield / valley membrane, hip-and-ridge cap shingles, pipe boots and step flashing.
Any shrinkage/damage/miscut contingency beyond the modest waste already built into the board and sheet counts.

shedking-16x20-gambrel-barn.caveats: ["This is PARTIAL, not fully priced. 81% of the LOW-end dollars come from a real, dated retailer price; only 43-52% of lines are retailer-verified at BOTH ends. 28 of 47 lines have an estimate on at least one end. Every estimated line is labelled 'ESTIMATE' in its source field. Do not treat the high end as a quote.", "Split of the number: the plan's own published materials list prices out at $6,450 (low) to $9,699 (high). I added $841-$1,506 of items the plan's list omits but which you cannot build without - roof deck sheathing, roof underlayment, the skids themselves, and exterior trim - to get the headline $7,289-$11,205. If you want the strict 'what the PDF lists' number, use $6,450-$9,699 ($20.16-$30.31/sq ft).", "THE PLAN'S MATERIALS LIST HAS REAL HOLES. It specifies 370 sq ft of shingles, drip edge, ridge cap and a ridge vent but lists ZERO sheets of roof sheathing. It lists '2x8x12 - 4 - Skid Bracing' but never lists the 4x6 skids the building sits on. It lists no trim, no door hardware, no handrail/guardrail, and no roofing underlayment. It also lists both 'Siding Underlayment' AND 'Tyvek Wrap' at the same square footage on all four walls, which is redundant - most builders would buy one or the other, saving ~$90.", "Home Depot dimensional lumber could NOT be priced. HD deliberately omits the price from the structured data on commodity lumber and sheet-goods pages; I tested ~15 lumber SKUs across 2025 and 2026 Wayback snapshots and every one returned $0.00. Lowe's returned no usable lumber product URLs at all. So the 'big-box premium' side of this range is carried by Menards, not HD/Lowe's.", "Surprising finding worth passing on: in 2026 a competitive yard and a big box are NOT reliably far apart on framing lumber, and the gap goes both ways. Menards' 2x6x16 ($15.54) undercut Sutherlands ($16.70), and Menards' LP SmartSide lap siding ($12.99) undercut Sutherlands ($14.28), while Menards was 10-16% higher on 2x6x8, 2x4x10 and 2x4x12. Architectural shingles at Menards ($34.70/bundle) came in cheaper than 3-tab at Sutherlands ($39.97). Anyone using a flat '+20% for big box' rule of thumb would be wrong here.", "Snapshot dates are mixed. Sutherlands prices are live as of 2026-09-07/08. Menards and Home Depot prices come from Wayback snapshots dated between 2025-01 and 2026-08; each is dated in the price_sources and priced_lines fields. Lumber is a commodity and moves; treat anything older than ~6 months as indicative.", "Sutherlands prices are per-store. I used store 3118 (Fredericksburg, TX); many prices were identical chain-wide but dimensional lumber is not. Sutherlands' default store (Harrisonville, MO) does not stock SPF and returns $0 - which is why the store parameter matters.", "Two spec substitutions on the low end: (a) the plan calls for 3ft x 4ft DOUBLE-hung windows and my verified $210 price is a SINGLE-hung TAFCO 36x48 - the double-hung units the plan specifies are the $310 high-end estimate; (b) truss gussets are specified as 1/2in plywood and my low end prices 7/16in OSB. Gussets are the structural heart of a site-built gambrel truss - buy the plywood.", "The door line swings $185 to $1,100 and it is the single largest source of spread. The plan includes door construction drawings, so building the 6ft double door from 2x4s and a sheet of siding is the intended path; the high figure is a purchased 72in unit. Pick one before you use this number.", "The waste factor is thin. I added 10% only to the lap siding. Real jobs lose 5-10% on nearly everything, and a gambrel with two 8ft-tall gable ends is a high-waste roof and siding shape. Add another 5-8% overall before you go to the yard.", "If your building department requires stamped trusses, the roof framing lines here (roughly $700 of 2x6, gussets, plates and nails) get replaced by a factory gambrel truss package at roughly $2,000-3,500 - which alone would push the top of this range past $12,500.", "Context this number is for: Best Barns' 16x20 kits sit at $11,190-$12,740 and a delivered/assembled 16x20 from Sheds Unlimited is quoted around $14,170. So the $29.95 plan plus a $7,300-$11,200 materials bill genuinely does undercut a kit - by roughly $1,500 to $5,400 at the low end - but only if you supply the labor, tools, scaffolding, foundation and permit yourself, none of which are in this figure."]
shedking-16x20-gambrel-barn.confidence: MEDIUM. High confidence on quantities: the entire bill of materials comes from Shedking's own 7-page public PDF (16x20-barn-materials.pdf, copyright 2024), read verbatim, so nothing is invented on the quantity side. High confidence on the framing, sheet-goods, siding, shingle and underlayment unit prices: those are real 2026 prices from two independent retailers, dated individually, cross-checked against each other and mostly within 10-16% of one another - which is itself evidence they are real. Confidence drops on the accessory tail (drip edge, soffit vents, ridge vent, mending plates, Simpson TWB bracing, joist-hanger nails, roofing nails, construction screws) where no retailer I could reach publishes a price, and on doors: that one line alone accounts for $915 of the $3,916 spread. The low end ($7,289) is the number I would stand behind - 81% of its dollars are retailer-verified and the material selections are ones I actually found in stock and priced. The high end ($11,205) is softer: it is built from grade upgrades plus the top of my estimate ranges, and it is NOT a big-box quote, because Home Depot and Lowe's lumber pricing was unobtainable from this host. A realistic single planning figure for a 2026 US build is about $8,500-$9,500 in materials, or $27-$30 per square foot, before foundation, delivery, tools and permit.
excludes: Foundation of any kind: concrete slab (the page offers it as an option), gravel pad, concrete piers/footings and the pier anchors the plan calls for, rebar, form lumber, sonotubes. A 16x20 4in slab is roughly 4 cu yd = $900-1,600 delivered in 2026, and gravel/excavation is extra.
Labor. This is a materials bill only. The plan involves 9 site-built 16ft-clear-span gambrel trusses, 2x12 loft framing, a full stair with landing, and 18ft 5-5/8in of working height.
Delivery. A 320 sq ft framing package is 3-4 tons and will not fit in a pickup; yard delivery is typically $75-250 per trip.

Tools and rentals: circular saw, framing nailer + compressor, roofing nailer, air hose, scaffolding or ladders (an 18ft-plus gambrel effectively requires scaffold rental), truss lifting help, safety gear.

Permit fees and plan review. Shedking's designer explicitly says he recommends a permit and that his truss drawings carry NO load limits or engineering, so a structural engineer's stamp may be required on top - typically $300-1,500 depending on jurisdiction.

Engineered trusses. The designer recommends buying engineered 16ft trusses from a truss plant rather than building them, for permit purposes. That would replace the 2x6x8/2x6x10/gusset/plate/nail lines here (roughly $700 of material) with a factory truss package - budget $2,000-3,500 for 11 gambrel trusses delivered.
Paint, primer, caulk, sealant, flashing tape, house-wrap tape. LP SmartSide comes primed but not finished; 768 sq ft of siding plus trim is 2 coats over ~900 sq ft.
Insulation, vapor barrier, interior wall/ceiling finish, interior paint, interior floor covering. The bill sheathes the loft floor and main floor in bare OSB/plywood.
Electrical: service feed, trenching, conduit, panel/subpanel, wire, boxes, receptacles, switches, fixtures, and the electrical permit.
Stair handrail, guardrail and loft edge rail - a full-size stair over 3ft wide plus a loft opening will need them for a permit, and the materials list contains none.
Gutters and downspouts, cupola material (free cupola plans are included with the plan but no materials are listed for it), ramp or steps up to the door threshold.
The $29.95 plan purchase itself, and sales tax on everything above.
